To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the nutritional ecology of maturing carnivores differs from that of mature adults.

(1) immature adults of a carnivorous beetle have a different nutritional ecology than mature adults; (2) immature adults have an intake target that differs from that of mature adults; and (3) immature adults have a different rule of compromise than mature adults.
the nutritional ecology of maturing insects differs from the nutritional ecology of mature insects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ecological factors influencing the evolution of life history traits.
how animals cope with nutritional challenges in their natural environments.
how organisms cope with nutritional stress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

“We have shown that, despite similar intake targets, immature adults and mature adults of the burying beetle Nicrophorus use different rules of compromise when restricted to protein or fat‐poor diets.”
the nutritional ecology of maturing carnivorous insects is complex, and it is not yet understood.

the rules of compromise for protein and fat are different in the immature and mature adults of the carnivore Nicrophorus, with immature adults behaving more like omnivore and mature adults more like carnivore.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rules of compromise are flexible, and can change with life stage.
we have shown that rules of compromise in a carnivorous beetle differ across life stages, with immature animals prioritizing protein intake, and mature animals prioritizing fat intake.

, despite having similar intake targets, immature and reproductively mature individuals of Nicrophorus show very different rules of compromise, with immature individuals showing strict regulation of dietary protein, resulting in obesity on protein‐poor foods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nutritional ecology of animals is highly labile, with different rules of compromise being followed by different stages in a life cycle.
the nutritional ecology of maturing insects is complex and can be very different from that of mature adults.

, although carnivores are known to be strict regulators of fat intake, this rule of compromise is labile across the life cycle, and can be overridden by a need to regulate protein intake in newly emerged adults.
